issues.problem: 类比把“暂缓扩张、先加固后方”等同于李左车计中的“断其辎重”。原计的“断辎重”是派奇兵去截断汉军（对方）的补给，不是加固己方后方；只有“坚壁不战”与“暂缓扩张、加固后方”大致对应。按现写法，读者会误解原计内容。

issues.rationale: 李左车计中的断辎重是派奇兵抄小路截断汉军（对方）的补给，与加固己方后方不对应；只有主力深沟高垒、坚营不战一项与暂缓扩张、加固后方大致对应。已删去括注中的断辎重，中文改为“深沟高垒、坚壁不战”，英文同步改为 dig in behind high walls and refuse battle，其余文字未动。

edits.before: Start with what Han Xin's army was up against. In the "Account of the Marquis of Huaiyin," one chapter of Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, Li Zuoche — the Lord of Guangwu — traces the Han army's road to Zhao: Han Xin crossed the Western River, captured the King of Wei, took Xia Yue alive, and fought a bloody battle at Yuyu; with Zhang Er now beside him he means to bring down Zhao. This is an army riding its victories far from home, and "its edge cannot be withstood." But Li Zuoche keeps a second ledger in the same breath: grain hauled a thousand li leaves soldiers with hunger on their faces; you cut firewood before you can cook, and no army stays fed. On the Jingxing road two carts cannot run abreast and cavalry cannot form a column; after several hundred li, the supplies must be somewhere behind. Strength and frailty were two faces of one army.
edits.after: Start with what Han Xin's army was up against. In the "Account of the Marquis of Huaiyin," one chapter of Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, Li Zuoche — the Lord of Guangwu — traces the Han army's road to Zhao: Han Xin crossed the Western River, captured the King of Wei, took Xia Yue alive, and fought a bloody battle at Yuyu; with Zhang Er now beside him he means to bring down Zhao. This is an army riding its victories far from home, and its edge, in his words, cannot be withstood. But Li Zuoche keeps a second ledger in the same breath: grain hauled a thousand li leaves soldiers with hunger on their faces; you cut firewood before you can cook, and no army stays fed. edits.before: His proposal followed from that. He asked to be lent thirty thousand picked troops to cut the Han baggage train by the side roads, while the main body held behind deep ditches and high walls and refused battle. Ahead the Han would have no one to fight; behind them no way back; with their rear cut and nothing to forage in the open country, he reckoned that in less than ten days the heads of the two generals could be delivered to the commander's tent. He closed with a warning: otherwise, he said, you will surely be taken by those two.

edits.before: 赵国这边的主帅成安君陈馀，史书对他的定性只有一句：「儒者也，常稱義兵不用詐謀奇計」。他拒绝的理由也被记了下来，是两层：一是算术，兵法说十倍可以围、倍数可以战，韩信号称数万、其实不过数千，千里奔袭已经疲惫到极点；二是名声，如果这样还避而不击，「則諸侯謂吾怯，而輕來伐我」。他没有采纳广武君的计策。
edits.after: 赵国这边的主帅成安君陈馀，本传在记他拒计时对他有这样一句定性：「儒者也，常稱義兵不用詐謀奇計」。他拒绝的理由也被记了下来，可以分成三层：一是算术，兵法说十倍可以围、倍数可以战，韩信号称数万、其实不过数千，千里奔袭已经疲惫到极点；二是往后，如果这样还避而不击，以后来了更强的敌人又怎么应付；三是名声，那样「則諸侯謂吾怯，而輕來伐我」。他没有采纳广武君的计策。

edits.before: Chen Yu, the Lord of Cheng'an and Zhao's commander-in-chief, gets one line of characterization from the historian: a Confucian, who always maintained that a righteous army does not use deceit and cunning schemes. His grounds for refusing are recorded too, in two layers. One is arithmetic: the manual says ten-to-one besieges, two-to-one fights; Han Xin claims tens of thousands but has no more than a few thousand, and a thousand-li raid has worn them to the bone. The other is reputation: to avoid battle at such odds would mean, in his words roughly, that the lords would think him cowardly and come lightly to attack him. He did not take the Guangwu Jun's advice.
edits.after: Chen Yu, the Lord of Cheng'an and Zhao's commander-in-chief, is characterized in this biography, at the point where he refuses the plan, as a Confucian who always maintained that a righteous army does not use deceit and cunning schemes. His grounds for refusing are recorded too, and they fall into three layers. One is arithmetic: the manual says ten-to-one besieges, two-to-one fights; Han Xin claims tens of thousands but has no more than a few thousand, and a thousand-li raid has worn them to the bone. The second looks ahead: if he avoided battle like this, how would he meet a stronger enemy that came later? The third is reputation: in his words roughly, the lords would then think him cowardly and come lightly to attack him. He did not take the Guangwu Jun's advice.

edits.before: The ambush had been waiting for exactly that. With the Zhao camp emptied, the two thousand riders swept in, pulled down the Zhao banners and raised two thousand red ones of Han. Beaten in front and unable to catch Han Xin, the Zhao troops turned for their camp and found "the walls were all hung with Han's red banners, and they were greatly alarmed," sure the Han had already taken the king of Zhao and his generals. The army dissolved; commanders cut men down to hold the line and could not. The Han struck from both sides, routed the Zhao army, killed the Lord of Cheng'an on the banks of the Zhi, and took King Xie alive.

edits.before: At the celebration the generals asked a question. The manual says to keep hills at the right rear and water at the left front; you ordered us to form up with our backs to the water, and said we would eat after Zhao was broken. We were not convinced — yet we won. What art is this? Han Xin's answer: it is in the manual; you simply failed to see it there. Does it not say "throw them onto death ground and they will live; place them where destruction is certain and they will survive"? The men I have are not old followers I have cared for over the years; this is what they call "driving men of the marketplace to fight." The situation demanded putting them on death ground, so that every man fought for his own life; give them ground to live in and they would all run, and then what use would they be? The generals conceded the point.

edits.before: 原文又记李左车说：「智者千慮，必有一失；愚者千慮，必有一得」，所以有句话说，狂夫之言，圣人也从中择取。一种解读是：一位刚刚亡国、被生擒的人，在这里讲的，近乎是任何人都可能出错——而他同时也说了，愚者也会有所得。
edits.after: 原文又记李左车说：「智者千慮，必有一失；愚者千慮，必有一得」，所以有句话说，狂夫之言，圣人也从中择取。这句话不是结局，而是献计前的铺垫：他接着说担心自己的计未必足用，但愿效愚忠，随即举成安君为例——有百战百胜之计，却「一旦而失之」，军败身死；然后献上自己的方案：按兵休整、镇抚赵地，再派辩士送信到燕国，向燕显示己方所长，并说「兵固有先聲而後實者」。韩信说「善」，「從其策」，派使者去燕，燕国「從風而靡」。一种解读是：他刚说的智者之失，紧接着就落在成安君身上；而韩信对出计者的对待，最后不只是礼遇，而是实际采用了他的计。

edits.before: The text also records Li Zuoche saying that the wise man, in a thousand considerations, must have one failure, and the fool, in a thousand considerations, must have one success — hence the saying, the sage still picks through a madman's words. One reading is that a man whose state had just fallen, taken alive, here suggests that anyone can be wrong — while also allowing that even a fool can be right.
edits.after: The text also records Li Zuoche saying that the wise man, in a thousand considerations, must have one failure, and the fool, in a thousand considerations, must have one success — hence the saying, the sage still picks through a madman's words. This was not the end but the preface to a plan. He went on to say he feared his plan might not be adequate but wished to offer his humble loyalty, and pointed to the Lord of Cheng'an, who had a plan that could win a hundred battles out of a hundred and lost it at a stroke, his army beaten and himself killed. Then he laid out his own proposal: rest the troops, settle Zhao, and send a persuader with a letter to Yan displaying Han's strengths, since in war there are times when reputation comes first and substance after. Han Xin said, Good, followed his plan, and sent an envoy to Yan; Yan bent like grass before the wind. One reading: the failure of the wise man he had just spoken of falls at once on the Lord of Cheng'an; and Han Xin's treatment of the adviser ended not merely in courtesy but in actually adopting his plan.

edits.before: 把原文所记陈馀拒绝的理由拆开看，会发现它们不是一类东西。「兵號數萬，其實不過數千」「千里而襲我，亦已罷極」是对敌情的判断，可以争论；“避而不击，诸侯就会说我怯懦”不是对汉军的判断，是对自身形象的判断。此外，史家在记这些理由之前，先交代了他平日的立场：「常稱義兵不用詐謀奇計」。这是司马迁对他一贯说法的描述，不是他这一次拒绝时给出的理由；而且它不是判断，是一条规矩。一种解释是：这条规矩与李左车的奇兵之计正好相冲，二者或有关联，但原文并没有把它记为这次拒绝的理由。作者推断，这也是为什么原文要给陈馀加上「儒者也」这个身份标签——史家记的是立场，不只是失策。

edits.before: Split apart the reasons the text records for Chen Yu's refusal and they are not the same kind of thing. Claims tens of thousands, really no more than a few thousand; a thousand-li raid has worn them to the bone — those are readings of the enemy, contestable in principle. Refuse battle and the lords will think me cowardly is not a reading of the Han army at all; it is a reading of his own image. Before recording those reasons, the historian also sets out his habitual stance: he always maintained that a righteous army does not use deceit and cunning schemes. That is Sima Qian's description of what Chen Yu habitually said, not a reason he gave for this refusal; and it is not a judgment at all but a rule. One explanation: that rule runs directly against Li Zuoche's surprise-force plan, and the two may be connected, but the text does not record it as a ground for this refusal. edits.before: Second detail worth holding onto: Han Xin did not march in on confidence. He advanced only after "sending men to look in on them and learning the plan had not been used." The rejected proposal was, in other words, one of the premises of his battle. The two thousand riders' success depended on the Zhao army emptying its camp to chase; the ten thousand men with the river at their backs were a separate arrangement. The author's inference is that this condition held only because Li Zuoche's plan had been shelved. One explanation: intelligence carried as much weight in this victory as formation. Han Xin first confirmed that his opponent would not listen to sound advice, then placed himself on the field.

edits.before: Han Xin put the conclusion more bluntly than anyone: it turned on "whether advice is used or not used, heeded or not heeded," and had the Lord of Cheng'an listened to you, I would be the captive.
